opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's been a pretty dramatic shift, honestly. When I started using the term "AGI" back in the early 2000s, along with Shane Legg and Peter Voss and a few others, it was a fringe thing. If you talked about building human-level thinking machines at an academic AI conference, people would look at you like you were a bit of a crank. The mainstream of the field had sort of retreated into narrow AI after the disappointments of the '70s and '80s. You'd work on a better classifier or a better planning algorithm for some specific domain, and the grand ambition of the founders of AI, people like Minsky and McCarthy, was considered embarrassing to bring up in polite company.

Now it's almost the opposite problem. Every big tech company says they're working toward AGI, and it's in the mission statements and the press releases. That has some really good effects. There's vastly more money, more talent, more compute, and more serious thinking going into the question of how you get from narrow systems to general intelligence. Young researchers can say "I want to work on AGI" without damaging their careers, and that's wonderful.

But there are downsides too. When something becomes fashionable, the term gets stretched. A lot of what's called AGI research now is really scaling up one particular paradigm, large neural models trained on huge datasets, and calling the result general intelligence because it can do a lot of impressive things. I think those systems are remarkable, but I don't think they have the kind of open-ended generalization, self-understanding, and ability to leap beyond their training that I'd consider the core of AGI. So the cultural acceptance has, in a way, narrowed the diversity of approaches, because the money flows to whatever is already working commercially.

And then there's the concentration issue, which I care a lot about. When AGI was a fringe pursuit, it was a scrappy community of open researchers. Now it's increasingly a race among a handful of very large corporations and governments. That raises real questions about who controls this technology and whose values it reflects. That's a big part of why I've pushed for decentralized approaches. If AGI is going to be as transformative as I think it will be, it really matters that it's not owned by a few entities.

So, net, I'm glad the field is taken seriously now. It means AGI is likely to come sooner. But it makes the questions about how it's developed, and by whom, a lot more urgent.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI was fringe and could damage careers, but does not explain that this selected for unusually dedicated or unconventional researchers.

r002.rationale: It links AGI’s increased acceptance with “vastly more money” going into the field, clearly indicating projects are easier to fund.

r003.rationale: It says acceptance narrowed the diversity of approaches, but does not say the mix of personalities became less interesting.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's been a remarkable shift, really. When I started using the term AGI, around 2002 or so, with Shane Legg and Cassio Pennachin and a few others, the whole topic was essentially disreputable. If you were an AI academic and you said you were working on human-level general intelligence, you'd get laughed out of the room, or at least you'd have a hard time getting grants or getting papers accepted. The field had been through the AI winters and everyone had retreated to narrow AI, to very specific applications, and the attitude was, we don't talk about the big goal anymore, we just do our incremental work and keep our heads down.

So for a long time AGI research was this small, somewhat marginal community. We started the AGI conference series in 2008 and it was a few dozen people, mostly fairly eccentric characters, myself included, with a lot of different theoretical approaches and not a lot of resources. And then, really over the last decade and especially the last few years, with deep learning and then the large language models, the whole thing flipped. Now AGI is in the mission statements of the biggest tech companies, it's in the newspapers, governments are talking about it. I find that both gratifying and a bit strange.

The positive side is obvious. There's a lot more money, a lot more talent, a lot more serious engineering effort going into the problem. Young researchers can say openly that they want to build thinking machines and nobody thinks they're crazy. That matters, because it means the smartest people can actually work on the thing that matters most instead of having to disguise it.

But there have been some costs too, I think. One is that the acceptance has been driven very much by one particular paradigm, large neural networks trained on massive data, and so the diversity of approaches that characterized the early AGI community has actually narrowed in some ways. There's a sort of homogenization. When AGI was marginal, people were exploring cognitive architectures, symbolic systems, evolutionary learning, neural-symbolic hybrids, all sorts of things. Now a huge fraction of the resources flow into scaling transformers. And my own view is that transformers alone aren't going to get us there, that you need something more like a hybrid architecture with real reasoning and memory and self-reflection, which is what we've been pursuing with OpenCog Hyperon. So I worry a bit that the mainstreaming has coupled the term AGI to a specific technology that may turn out to be a stepping stone rather than the destination.

The other thing is the centralization. In the early days, AGI research was open, it was done by small teams and academics sharing ideas. Now the frontier work is happening inside a handful of very large corporations, largely behind closed doors, and the motivation is as much commercial and competitive as it is scientific. That's part of why I've put so much energy into decentralized approaches, SingularityNET and so forth, because I think who builds the first AGI and under what governance structure may matter as much as the technical details.

And then there's the cultural discourse itself, which has become quite polarized. You have the people who think AGI is imminent and will save us all, and the people who think it's imminent and will kill us all, and there's a lot of heat and not always a lot of careful thinking. Whereas in the old, marginal days, we could have these long, relaxed discussions about consciousness and cognitive architecture and ethics without anyone's stock price depending on the outcome.

So on balance I'm glad the field is taken seriously now. I spent a lot of years arguing that it should be. But I'd like to see the seriousness come with more intellectual openness and more plurality of approaches, rather than everyone piling onto the same bandwagon.

r001.rationale: The response describes career barriers and a small, marginal community of eccentric researchers, but does not say those risks selected for unusually dedicated or unconventional people.

r002.rationale: It says greater acceptance brought “a lot more money” and more resources into AGI research.

r003.rationale: It describes a narrowing of research approaches and calls early researchers eccentric, but does not say the changing acceptance made the field’s mix of personalities less interesting.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think it’s changed the field quite dramatically. For a long time, if you said you were working on artificial general intelligence, people would look at you as though you were a little crazy. You could work on a particular learning algorithm or a particular application, but saying that your actual goal was to build a machine that could think and learn as broadly as a human was liable to hurt your credibility. So having that become a legitimate ambition opens up funding, attracts talented people, and lets researchers talk more honestly about what they’re trying to accomplish.

But there’s a flip side. Once AGI becomes fashionable, people start applying the label to whatever they were already doing. And you can get a tremendous concentration of resources around approaches that have demonstrated commercial success, without necessarily having demonstrated that they can get all the way to general intelligence.

So I think the cultural shift is very positive overall. We can have the discussion openly now. But acceptance of the goal isn’t the same thing as understanding how to achieve it. We still need room for different architectures, different theories, and ideas that don’t fit the current consensus.

r001.rationale: It says pursuing AGI could hurt researchers’ credibility, but does not explain that this career risk selected for unusually dedicated or unconventional researchers.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says legitimacy for AGI opens up funding.

r003.rationale: It discusses AGI becoming fashionable and resources concentrating around commercially successful approaches, but does not suggest the field’s mix of personalities has become less interesting.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think it’s changed the field quite dramatically. For a long time, if you said you were working on artificial general intelligence, people would assume you were either confused or doing something that wasn’t really respectable science. You could work on a very narrow piece of the problem, but saying explicitly that your goal was a machine that could think and learn broadly was almost a liability.

Now you can state that goal openly, and that makes it much easier to attract talented people, get funding, and have serious discussions across different areas of research. That’s a very positive development.

But cultural acceptance doesn’t mean we’ve resolved the scientific questions. There’s a tendency for people to take whatever approach is currently successful and assume that scaling it up will give us AGI. And maybe scaling is part of the answer, but we should keep a broad range of ideas alive. To me, the real opportunity is to use this new openness to explore the problem more deeply, rather than letting the field converge prematurely on one recipe.

r002.rationale: It says that openly stating the goal of AGI now makes it much easier to get funding.
